title: Rethinking Fast and Slow
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Recent research challenges the Thinking, Fast and Slow framework by revealing that for a significant class of problems, correct intuitive answers often precede deliberation rather than requiring it. Using the Compound Remote Associates test, researchers found that 70 percent of correct final answers had been intuitively correct in the initial response. Good intuition depends not on processing power but on having richly interconnected semantic memory where knowledge is well organized. Success in creative problem solving correlates with semantic networks that have shorter path lengths between concepts and flexible associations—structure matters more than quantity of knowledge. This suggests intelligence is not fixed at birth but partly cultivated through accumulated experience and knowledge organization. Deliberation remains important when problems exceed intuitive capacity, but the takeaway reframes good thinking: it may consist less in overriding bad intuitions and more in building knowledge structures that produce sound intuitions automatically.
points: Good intuition depends on semantic memory structure, not processing power; the way knowledge is organized matters more than how much you know
When participants gave correct final answers after deliberation, they had already generated the correct answer intuitively 70 percent of the time
Individuals with more interconnected, flexible semantic networks displayed higher rates of correct intuitive responding
Intelligence is partly constructible rather than fixed; semantic architecture is built through experience and reflection
Deliberation is not the universal engine of correctness; it becomes necessary only when automatic processes reach their limits
quotes: If intuition, properly structured, can reliably produce correct answers without deliberation, then the goal of education cannot simply be to teach students to think more slowly and carefully.
The decisive cognitive work appears to have happened before deliberation even starts. Intuition, here, is not a rash shortcut waiting to be corrected by reason.

Sound thinkers are not primarily characterised by their capacity to correct intuitive errors through deliberation. Rather, they appear to be distinguished by their ability to intuit correctly in the first place.
If intelligence is partly a matter of how knowledge is organised, then it is partly a matter of what can be learned.
What appears as natural talent could be the visible surface of invisible preparation.” Archived from The Learning Dispatch on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
